INSTANTANEOUS ROUND-UP VIEWS.

articles.headline: Thanksgiving Proclamation. A Proclamation by the Governor.
articles.text:
During the season that has passed, the people of this territory have been abundantly blessed with health and freedom from distressing calamities;

The hand of justice has not been stayed;

The laws have been observed;

No social disturbance has afflicted us;

No angry turmoil has rent communities in twain or called for force to maintain order.

Though the fullest fruits of American citizen-ship have not yet been attained, no people are less burdened with legal restrictions, and no freer breath is drawn than that enjoyed by the citizens of this common-wealth. Safe in his home! Safe in the enjoyment of his conscience and his God!

For these and for kindred blessings it is becoming that we raise our voices in gratitude to the Almighty.

Therefore, in conformity to the president's proclamation, I commend to the people the observance of Thursday, the 25th day of November, as a day of thanksgiving and prayer. "With malice toward none, with charity for all," remembering the needy and afflicted, and beseeching the Divine blessing on the future of this land, let us meet in church and home and celebrate this annual festival—a season associated with sacred memories and hallowed by the custom of our fathers.

"Under God the people rule."

Witness my hand and the great seal of the Territory, this 4th day of November, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and eignty six.

GILBERT A. PIERCE.

SEAL.

By the Governor:

M. L. MCCORMACK, Secretary.
articles.summary: Dakota Territory Governor Gilbert A. Pierce's proclamation, dated November 4, 1886, naming Thursday, November 25 a day of thanksgiving and prayer.

articles.text: The Chicago Inter Ocean figures the cost of the butchers' strike at $2,000,000.
articles.summary: The Chicago Inter Ocean puts the cost of the butchers' strike at $2,000,000.

articles.text: Telegrams yesterday reported heavy snow-storms all over Minnesota. It was not stated whether the storm was going east or west.
articles.summary: Telegrams reported heavy snowstorms across Minnesota.

articles.text: Sullivan and Ryan had their "go" in San Francisco last Monday, Ryan being knocked out in the third round. It appears that the exponent of Boston "culchah" has not yet been downed by John Barleycorn.
articles.summary: Comment on the Sullivan–Ryan prize fight in San Francisco, which Ryan lost in the third round.

articles.text: The Bismarck Tribune announces that navigation on the Missouri river closed yesterday, and that this year has been disagreeable and discouraging for the boats. The Batchelor, Rosebud, Helena and General Terry are now in winter quarters at Bismarck.
articles.summary: The Bismarck Tribune reports Missouri River navigation closed for the season, with four steamboats wintering at Bismarck.

articles.text: Next to Kansas, Dakota has had more miles of railroad laid within her borders this year than has any state or territory in the union. It is confidently expected that next year will witness an even greater number of miles laid.
articles.summary: Dakota ranked second only to Kansas in new railroad mileage laid in 1886.
A short editorial reacting to a report from Florida that Apache prisoners of Geronimo's band were dying at a rate of four a day, and declaring they should have been hanged when captured.

articles.text: The Custer battle field or at least the township in which the Custer monument is located, will be turned into a military reservation by the president's order in the near future. Whatever can be said of Custer's judgment, he was an honest able and fearless officer and this recognition of his memory by the government although tardy, will be welcomed by Custer's many friends in this part of the country.
articles.summary: The township containing the Custer monument is to be made a military reservation by presidential order; the paper welcomes the recognition.

articles.text: A whole host of rumors is rolling westward concerning the present visit of Governor Pierce to Washington. The most of them have as a basis, that he is to be removed and a democrat appointed in his place. If Grover Cleveland is gifted with even ordinary common sense, and it must be an offensive partisan indeed who will not concede him that much, Governor Pierce's seat is as secure as that of the president himself. Although Governor Pierce has repeatedly placed his office at the disposal of the administration, President Cleveland will not dare to go back on his civil service views in such a prominent office as that of Dakota's governor. Either Pierce will resign peremptorily or he will serve out his term of office.
articles.summary: The paper dismisses rumors that Governor Pierce, visiting Washington, will be replaced by a Democrat, predicting he will either resign or serve out his term.

articles.text: At last the butchers' strike in Chicago is ended the men have returned to work under the ten-hour-a-day rule. At least six or eight thousand men had been hired meantime however, and they will permanently take the place of that number of strikers. Already thousands of the old men have been refused work as the packers are now full-handed. The strike was inaugurated over the eight-hour rule, the packers finding it absolutely impossible to run profitably paying ten hours wages for eight hours work and selling their product in the same market in competition with men who paid even
articles.summary: The Chicago packinghouse strike has ended with workers back under the ten-hour day; item continues at the top of column 6.

articles.text: a less price for ten hours' work. The packers announced their intention of returning to the ten-hour system and the employes of the stock-yards to the number of 15,000 or more, struck. The packers declared their intention of shutting sooner than yield and thus the matter stood for ten days before Monday. Meantime the packers had been getting in several thousands of men from outside cities and all were running though short-handed. Saturday or Sunday a telegram came from Grand Master Workman Powderly that the men should return to work under the ten-hour system or that their charters as Knights of Labor should be taken away. As a result, enough of the strikers have applied for places to run the packing-houses to their full capacity and thousands more are out of employment, with a hard winter staring them in the face. This is the unfortunate side of the affair and it is to be much regretted that a few hot-heads could lead the majority to a strike that has ended so disastrously to them. We believe as thoroughly as any one in the eight-hour rule but we do not believe it is just for the workmen of one house or of one city in any branch of business to demand eight hours' work and ten hours' pay when their employers must compete in open market with men who are paying recognized wages for a recognized days' work. To be just the movement must be unanimous or fail.
articles.summary: Continuation (from column 5) of an editorial on the end of the Chicago packing-house strike, after Powderly ordered Knights of Labor men back to work on the ten-hour system; the Cow Boy favors the eight-hour rule only if adopted unanimously.

articles.text: The Indians at Standing Rock are said by the Bismarck Tribune to have just had a formal unveiling of the standing rock from which the post takes its name. The ceremonies were very impressive from an Indian standpoint and are told in full in the Tribune. We are a little "jubersome" however, as to the foundation for the article. "Brer. Quinson" is back on the Tribune as local editor, Bismarck is a little dull, the columns of the Tribune must be filled;—well on the whole, it looks like a first-rate attempt at "filling."
articles.summary: The Cow Boy doubts a Bismarck Tribune report of a formal unveiling of the standing rock at Standing Rock, suggesting returning local editor "Brer. Quinson" invented it to fill columns.

articles.text: A large number of steers in the Chicago Fat Stock show run over 2,000 pounds, the heaviest being McGregor, 2,560 pounds. This show is yearly creating greater interest in stock circles, and from it has sprung many valuable ideas in the stock business. The attendance this year was larger than usual and the most intense interest has been manifested. The butterine men came out in full force in their display and made many converts to the healthfulness of their product.
articles.summary: Notes on the Chicago Fat Stock show: heavy steers (McGregor at 2,560 pounds), large attendance, and a butterine display.

articles.text: The Hereford men have made rapid strides toward popularity lately, the climax being the winning of the sweepstakes prize by Rudolph, Jr., a Hereford at the Chicago Fat Stock show. He is 883 days old and weighs 1,530 pounds, an average daily gain of 1.73 pounds. The Hereford men are jubilant, as the prize was won over remarkably fine animals of the Shorthorn, Polled-Angus Holstein, Devon and Sussex breeds. The Hereford Association have petitioned Congress to forbid all importation of cattle for one year in order to the better extirpate pleuro-pneumonia from the United States.
articles.summary: The Hereford steer Rudolph, Jr. won the sweepstakes at the Chicago Fat Stock show, and the Hereford Association petitioned Congress for a one-year ban on cattle imports to fight pleuro-pneumonia.

articles.headline: The American Cowboy.
articles.summary: Reprinted article (credited at its end in column 7 to Joseph Nimmo, Jr., in Harper's Magazine) describing how the northern-range cowboy differs from the original Texas cowboy, noting that many ranch proprietors are Easterners and wealthy Europeans, some titled, drawn to the cattle business. It goes on to describe the organization and discipline of the new northern range outfits; not transcribed per instructions.

articles.text: The cattle-shipping season is nearly ended, but it seems as though there were never more freight trains running than there are at present.
articles.summary: Cattle shipping nearly over but freight traffic heavy.

articles.text: Postals have been sent out to all Billings county's tax-payers, stating the amount of their taxes and conveying a polite intimation that it is time to settle up.
articles.summary: Billings county taxpayers sent tax notices.

articles.text: J. W. Foley who is now here will probably take charge of the Medora interests of the N. P. Ref. Car Co. this winter, W. F. Van Driesche contemplating a trip to Europe.
articles.summary: J. W. Foley likely to take charge of the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co.'s Medora interests while W. F. Van Driesche goes to Europe.

articles.text: The Maltese Cross, Quarter-circle diamond and KC outfits started on a bull round-up Monday, which will last for several days yet. The object is to gather in the young bulls and weak cows that need feeding.
articles.summary: The Maltese Cross, Quarter-circle diamond and KC outfits began a bull round-up.

articles.text: The school tax for this year in the Medora precinct, is ten mills, which will leave a surplus for next years' expenses. All other taxes for county and territorial purposes, amount to ten and nine-tenths mills.
articles.summary: Medora precinct school tax is ten mills; other taxes 10.9 mills.

articles.text: George W. Fowler, agent and correspondent for the Bismarck Tribune, is in town to-day. The daily Tribune will be sent until March 1 for $2, making it the cheapest and most valuable daily for this part of the country.
articles.summary: Bismarck Tribune agent George W. Fowler is in Medora.

articles.text: Several papers are making mention of remarkable veins of coal in their locality, some going as high as twenty feet. The Bad Lands still takes the lead however in the vein of coal on Deep creek at Mattox' ranch. It is over sixty feet thick in plain sight from the top to the bed of the creek. How much deeper it is no one knows.
articles.summary: A coal vein over sixty feet thick is exposed on Deep creek at Mattox' ranch.

articles.text: The fight over the elections is not ended in Stark county. It will be remembered Trask, according to the returns, had a majority of one over Sebastian. The election was then contested by Mr. Sebastian and it appears with good prospect of succeess, although the courts will be called on to decide the case, no matter how it is decided by the county canvassing board.
articles.summary: Sebastian is contesting Trask's one-vote win in a Stark county election.

articles.text: M. F. Mullins one of the butchers here last summer, won first prize at the recent butchers' contests at the Chicago Fat-Stock show over six other competitors, supposed to be the most skillful in the United States. Mullins' time was ten minutes and seventeen seconds, beating Noonan, another old butcher here, who left in August, by sixteen seconds. Noonan won second prize by twelve seconds.
articles.summary: Former Medora butchers M. F. Mullins and Noonan took first and second prizes at the Chicago Fat-Stock show butchers' contest.

articles.text: Our little flurry of snow three weeks ago, which passed off almost as quickly as it came, was perhaps a harbinger of the disastrous snow storms that have blockaded business in some parts of Indiana, Michigan, New York and eastern states. In many places the snow was from a foot to twenty inches deep on a level, the drifts being from three to ten feet. We doubt if there is now a particle of snow in Dakota and the weather during the day is simply perfect.
articles.summary: Contrasts eastern snowstorms with fine snow-free weather in Dakota.

articles.text:
To close out the stock of Studebaker wagons now on hand, I will make prices for cash that are lower than the wholesale factory rate. The wagons are new and first-class and have Studebaker Bros. full guarantee as to soundness. They will be sold cheaper than any wagons that have ever been sold in this country and cheaper than they can be bought in car lots at the factory. The only reason for making these rates is to close out stock on hand. They must and shall go soon.

A. T. Packard.
articles.summary: Packard offers his Studebaker wagon stock below factory rate to close it out.
